hints: Focus on the gas released, it is carbon dioxide, so start by thinking how to turn a gas volume at room conditions into moles.
Convert $200 \text{ cm}^3$ into moles using $24000 \text{ cm}^3$ per mole, then remember 1 mole of any carbonate gives 1 mole of $\text{CO}_2$.
Use $M_r = \text{mass} \div \text{moles}$ to find the molar mass of the unknown carbonate, then see which metal makes that total work.
walkthrough:
**Find moles of carbon dioxide released**

Think simply, the acid is in excess so all the carbonate reacts. The amount of gas tells us the amount of carbonate we started with.

Chemical rule for room conditions:
$$\text{moles of gas} = \frac{\text{volume in cm}^3}{24000}$$

**Calculate the moles**

Put in the numbers from the question. It is a lovely easy division if you look carefully.
$$n(\text{CO}_2) = \frac{200}{24000} = 0.00833 \text{ mol}$$

**Link moles of gas to moles of carbonate**

Both Group 1 and Group 2 carbonates give one $\text{CO}_2$ per carbonate, so the ratio is 1 to 1.
$$\text{M}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{MCl} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{MCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MCl}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$n(\text{carbonate}) = n(\text{CO}_2) = 0.00833 \text{ mol}$$

**Find the $M_r$ and identify the metal**

Molar mass is just mass divided by moles. This is the key step that identifies the compound.
$$M_r = \frac{0.833}{0.00833} \approx 100$$
Subtract the mass of $\text{CO}_3$ ($12.0 + 3 \times 16.0 = 60.0$) to leave about 40 for the metal. That matches calcium ($40.1$), so the carbonate is $\text{CaCO}_3$.

options.A: Incorrect. $M_r$ of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = (2 \times 23.0) + 12.0 + (3 \times 16.0) = 106$. This would give moles $= 0.833 \div 106 = 0.00786$ mol and only about $189 \text{ cm}^3$ of $\text{CO}_2$, less than observed.
options.B: Incorrect. $M_r$ of $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 = (2 \times 39.1) + 12.0 + (3 \times 16.0) = 138.2$. This is much too heavy, so 0.833 g would be only about 0.006 mol and release only about $145 \text{ cm}^3$ of gas.
options.C: Incorrect. $M_r$ of $\text{MgCO}_3 = 24.3 + 12.0 + (3 \times 16.0) = 84.3$. This is too light, so 0.833 g would be about 0.0099 mol and release about $237 \text{ cm}^3$ of gas, more than observed.
options.D: Correct. $M_r$ of $\text{CaCO}_3 = 40.1 + 12.0 + (3 \times 16.0) = 100.1$. Moles $= 0.833 \div 100.1 = 0.00832$ mol, which gives $0.00832 \times 24000 = 200 \text{ cm}^3$ of $\text{CO}_2$, exactly matching the experiment.
